stories.headline: Sheikh Hasina asks Bangladesh for a passport to return home
stories.question: Why does Sheikh Hasina want a new passport, and what if she leaves India?
stories.dek: Bangladesh revoked Hasina's old passport, so she needs new papers to go home on her own. Dhaka refuses to issue them and says India must hand her over instead. India has not agreed.

so_far.text: Sheikh Hasina was still Bangladesh's prime minister when she fled to India in 2024, during a student-led uprising. In August 2024, Bangladesh's interim government revoked her diplomatic passport. Later, a Bangladeshi war-crimes court, the International Crimes Tribunal, sentenced her to death in absentia, meaning without her being present. It found she ordered a deadly crackdown on the uprising. She denies the charges. Her party, the Awami League, is banned. After the verdict in November 2025, Bangladesh formally asked India to extradite her under a 2013 treaty. India said it was examining the request.

what_happened.text: Reuters reported on 9 November 2026 that Hasina has asked for a new Bangladeshi passport and national ID card so she can return. Reuters says this is her first such communication since she fled. Her London lawyers, Matrix Chambers, emailed the Bangladesh High Commission in New Delhi, addressed to its head, Preeti Rahman. Aides say a December return is planned, and Hasina says she will surrender before a court. On 5 November, Bangladesh's State Minister for Foreign Affairs, Humaiun Kobir, said no ordinary passport or travel document will be issued. He called her a 'fugitive' and said India must hand her over.

steps.text: To cross a border lawfully, a person needs a passport or travel document issued by their own country.
Bangladesh revoked Hasina's diplomatic passport in August 2024, so she has no valid papers to fly home herself.
Dhaka refuses a new passport because it wants her returned by extradition, a formal handover by India.
India has not agreed, and the 2013 treaty excludes political offences, which can complicate a handover.
If she did return, she says she would surrender to a court, where a death sentence already stands against her.

lesson.concept: How extradition between two countries works
lesson.big_idea: Extradition is one country formally handing a wanted person to another. It needs a treaty, a request and the host country's yes. The only other way home is to travel back yourself, with valid papers.

steps.title: A treaty is a standing promise
steps.text: Two countries sign an extradition treaty, a written promise to hand back people wanted for crimes. Without one, the host country has no duty to act. India and Bangladesh have such a treaty, signed in 2013.

steps.title: The request goes through diplomats
steps.text: The country that wants the person sends a formal request, often a note verbale, a written note between governments. Bangladesh sent one through its high commission in Delhi after the November 2025 verdict.

steps.title: Exceptions can block a handover
steps.text: Treaties list reasons a country may refuse. The India–Bangladesh treaty excludes political offences, meaning crimes seen as political acts. Some observers say a death sentence also complicates a handover. Interpretations differ.

steps.title: The host country decides
steps.text: Usually the host country's courts examine the case, and its government makes the final call. Until then, the person stays where they are. India earlier said Bangladesh's request was under legal and judicial examination, and it has not agreed.

steps.title: Going home alone needs papers
steps.text: Extradition is a forced handover. A person can instead travel home on their own, but only with a valid passport or travel document. Only their own country can issue that document.

example.setup: Imagine Ravi, a former mayor in Country A, is convicted there while he lives in Country B. Country A wants him back. Let's follow both routes home.

lines.label: Route 1: treaty
lines.calc: A and B have an extradition treaty
lines.note: Without it, B has no duty to act.

lines.label: Formal request
lines.calc: A sends B a diplomatic note
lines.note: This starts the handover process.

lines.label: Exception check
lines.calc: Ravi says the case is political
lines.note: B must weigh the political-offence exclusion.

lines.label: B decides
lines.calc: B's courts examine; B's government says yes or no
lines.note: Until then, Ravi stays in B.

lines.label: Route 2: go home
lines.calc: Ravi asks A for a new passport
lines.note: Only A can issue it.

lines.label: A refuses
lines.calc: No passport, so Ravi cannot travel himself
lines.note: A insists B must hand him over.

example.result: A handover needs Country B's yes. A trip home on his own needs Country A's passport. Each country holds one key, so if both hold back, Ravi stays stuck in B.

apply.text: This is Hasina's position. Bangladesh asked India to extradite her in November 2025. India has not agreed and is watching developments. The treaty excludes political offences. So Hasina tried Route 2: a passport to return and surrender to a court. Bangladesh's Humaiun Kobir said no passport will be issued, and India must hand her over.

practice.q: Suppose Country A changes its mind and gives Ravi a passport while B is still examining the extradition request. Can Ravi go home, and does B still need to decide?
practice.answer: Route 2 is now open. Ravi has valid papers, so, assuming B has not detained him, he can travel home himself. Extradition is a forced handover, so if he leaves on his own, B no longer has a request to decide. Back in A, he faces A's courts.

stories.headline: China's factory prices jump 5.7%, but its shoppers barely feel it
stories.question: China's factory prices are rising fastest in four years. Is China now exporting inflation?
stories.dek: Not broadly, on the evidence so far. Coal, oil and gas drive the jump, along with a low starting point last year. Weak demand at home stops firms passing costs on, so consumer prices barely moved.

so_far.text: China's producer price index, or PPI, tracks what factories charge for goods as they leave the factory. For about three and a half years it kept falling. A long fall in prices is called deflation. The Iran war began at the end of February 2026, and oil prices climbed. Factory prices then started rising and have now gone up for eight months in a row. China's economy grew 4.5% in the third quarter, helped by strong exports. Household spending has recovered only slowly.

what_happened.text: On 9 November 2026 China's National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) published its price data for October. The PPI rose 5.7% from a year earlier. In September it had risen 5.0%. This is the fastest rise since June 2022. Input prices, what factories pay for raw materials, rose 7.9%. Consumer prices, measured by the consumer price index (CPI), rose just 0.7%. That was down from 0.9% in September and below the 0.8% forecast. Core CPI, which leaves out food and energy, was 0.8%, matching this year's low.

steps.text: The Iran war pushed oil prices up, so coal mining prices rose 36.6% and oil and gas extraction 35.0%.
Nine industries, led by coal mining, oil and gas extraction, and fuel processing, added over 6 percentage points to the PPI rise.
The PPI fell 2.1% in October 2025, so October 2026 is compared with a low level. That makes the rise look bigger.
Households are cautious and housing is in a long slump, so firms cannot pass higher costs on to buyers.
So costs rise faster than selling prices. Factory profit margins get squeezed, and shop prices barely move.

Factory prices of Chinese consumer goods have fallen for over three years. Only half of 30 key industries saw price rises. lesson.concept: How rising costs travel from mine to shop
lesson.big_idea: Prices move along a chain: raw materials, then factory goods, then shop shelves. A cost rise reaches shoppers only if each seller can charge more. When buyers are weak, firms absorb it.

steps.title: Start with input prices
steps.text: Factories buy raw materials such as coal, oil and chemicals. What they pay are called input prices. In China these rose 7.9% in October from a year earlier.

steps.title: Then the factory-gate price
steps.text: The factory sells its goods at the factory gate. The producer price index (PPI) tracks these prices. China's PPI rose 5.7% in October.

steps.title: Then the shop price
steps.text: Shops buy from factories and sell to you. The consumer price index (CPI) tracks what households pay. China's CPI rose only 0.7% in October.

steps.title: Passing on needs willing buyers
steps.text: Each seller can raise prices only if buyers still pay. In China, cautious households and a housing slump mean firms cannot pass costs on, so the rise stalls along the chain.

steps.title: Watch the starting point
steps.text: A year-on-year figure compares this month with the same month last year. If last year was unusually low, the jump looks bigger. China's PPI fell 2.1% in October 2025.

example.setup: Say a small factory pays ₹100 for the materials in one kettle and sells it for ₹120. Then its material costs rise 10%, but buyers will accept only a 5% higher price.

lines.label: Old margin
lines.note: Profit per kettle before the cost shock

lines.label: New input cost
lines.note: Materials get dearer, like China's input prices

lines.label: New selling price
lines.note: Buyers resist, so the price rises less than costs

lines.label: New margin
lines.note: The factory absorbs part of the cost

lines.label: Margin change
lines.note: This is a squeezed margin

example.result: Costs rose 10%, but the buyer saw only 5%. The factory kept less profit on each kettle. That is how a cost shock can stay mostly inside factories instead of reaching shop shelves.

apply.text: China looks like the kettle factory. Input prices rose 7.9%, but factory selling prices rose only 5.7%, the widest gap in four months. Shoppers saw just 0.7%. With households cautious, firms cannot pass costs on. So the energy shock stays mostly inside industry, not in what Chinese consumers pay.

practice.q: Same factory: costs ₹100, price ₹120. Now costs rise 20% and buyers accept a 10% higher price. What is the new margin?
practice.answer: New cost: ₹100 + 20% = ₹120. New price: ₹120 + 10% = ₹132. New margin: ₹132 − ₹120 = ₹12. The margin falls from ₹20 to ₹12, a 40% squeeze.

check.why: Costs rose faster than selling prices, so the gap per unit shrank. Shoppers saw only a 0.7% rise.

takeaways: A cost rise reaches shoppers only if each seller can charge more; otherwise margins shrink.
China's factory prices rose 5.7% on energy costs, but its consumer prices rose only 0.7%.
Watch oil: Capital Economics expects the shock to fade in 2027, with factory prices falling again.

stories.headline: France blames Iran's Revolutionary Guards for hacking supermarket fridges
stories.question: How could Iran hack the fridges in French supermarkets, and why would it?
stories.dek: The attackers got into fridge control panels that were reachable over the internet and running outdated software. Then they turned up the heat. France blames Iran's Revolutionary Guards. The motive has not been stated.

so_far.text: Overnight on 11–12 October 2026, fridges and freezers in hundreds of French supermarkets suddenly heated up. France's cyber agency, ANSSI, found a weakness in software from Danfoss, a Danish firm. On 9 August, the security firm Claroty had published research showing a way to get past the login on Danfoss systems. Another security firm, Sekoia, said stores in Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany and Belgium were also affected. On 2 November, similar overnight temperature spikes hit stores in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Luxembourg and Sweden. France and Iran were already at odds. On 19 August, France had expelled two Iranian embassy employees.

what_happened.text: On 9 November, French foreign minister Jean-Noël Barrot said the October attack was carried out by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). He called it the first large-scale cyberattack for sabotage purposes on French soil. French authorities are investigating Shahid Kaveh, an attack-focused cyber unit linked to the IRGC. The Paris prosecutor has asked for international arrest warrants for its leader and two deputies. Investigators say the attackers used Farsi, the Persian language, and IP addresses linked to devices in Iran. France summoned Iran's ambassador and promised sanctions at European level. The Wall Street Journal reports that the US also suspects Iran. Iran did not respond right away.

steps.text: Supermarket fridges are run by control panels. Many of these panels could be reached over the internet for remote management.
Research published on 9 August showed how to get past the login on Danfoss systems. The units hit ran outdated firmware.
Once inside, the attackers raised temperatures to as high as 50°C and forced defrosting. The stock spoiled overnight.
Investigators traced Farsi and Iranian IP addresses. So France blamed the IRGC and is investigating its Shahid Kaveh unit.
No source states a motive. France and Iran have quarrelled for months, but no link to the attack is confirmed.

for_you.text: No reports so far say India has been affected. Indian stores, prices and travel are not directly touched. The lesson still applies here. Any machine run over the internet can be hijacked if its software is out of date. That includes a cold store, a water pump or an office's air conditioning. In this case, the damage came from the fridge panels, not from the shops' main computers.

misconception.fact: Here, attackers went straight into the fridge control panels, which could be reached over the internet. Danfoss said the affected panels were running outdated firmware.

lesson.concept: How hackers take over internet-connected machines
lesson.big_idea: Any machine you can control over the internet, an attacker can try to control too. A known flaw that nobody fixes becomes an open door.

steps.title: Fridges have small computers
steps.text: A supermarket fridge is run by a control panel. This is a small computer that sets the temperature and decides when to defrost, which means melting built-up ice.

steps.title: Connecting them to the internet
steps.text: Putting the panel online lets technicians check and adjust fridges from anywhere. But it also means anyone on the internet can try to log in. In this attack, the panels hit could be reached online.

steps.title: A flaw that skips the login
steps.text: An authentication bypass is a flaw that lets someone get in without the password. On 9 August, the security firm Claroty published research on such flaws in Danfoss systems.

steps.title: Fixes only work if installed
steps.text: Makers fix flaws by releasing new firmware, the device's built-in software. A device that never gets the update stays open. Danfoss said the units hit were running outdated firmware.

steps.title: Inside, attackers change settings
steps.text: Once in, an attacker can change any setting a technician could. In October, attackers raised temperatures to as high as 50°C and forced defrosting.

example.setup: Imagine 1,000 supermarkets, each with a fridge panel online. A login flaw is published, and the maker releases a fix. Assume 800 stores install the update in time.

lines.note: Scanning tools can search the whole internet quickly.

lines.note: One night of heat ruins all the stock.

example.result: Even when 80% of stores update, the remaining 20% are enough for a wide attack. The fix protects only the stores that install it, and attackers look for the ones that didn't.

practice.q: Suppose a chain has 400 stores with fridge panels online, and only half install the update. How many stay exposed, and what are two ways to protect them?
practice.answer: Half of 400 is 200, so 200 stores update. 400 − 200 = 200 panels stay exposed. Way one: install the firmware update. Way two: take the panels off the open internet so attackers can't reach them.

stories.headline: TRAI caps the fees telecom companies pay to link networks
stories.question: TRAI is capping the fees telecom companies pay each other. Will your phone bill change?
stories.dek: Probably not directly. Operators charge each other these wholesale fees for network links. No source says tariffs will change. From 1 January 2027, the caps set clear upper limits on these costs.

so_far.text: When you call someone on a different network, the call must cross from one company's network into the other's. That meeting point is called an interconnection. The link plugs into a "port", and operators pay each other charges for these ports. TRAI, the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India, last revised port charges in 2012. Those rules were built for old E1/TDM ports, an older circuit-based technology. TRAI began a review with a pre-consultation paper on 3 April 2025. A consultation paper followed on 10 November 2025, and an open house on 28 January 2026.

what_happened.text: On 9 November 2026 TRAI released the Telecommunication Interconnection (Port Charges) (Third Amendment) Regulations, 2026. They cap the yearly charge for an IP-based interconnection port at ₹5.6 lakh for a 1 Gbps port and ₹42.3 lakh for a 10 Gbps port. The caps take effect on 1 January 2027. They apply the same way to fixed-line, mobile, national long-distance and international long-distance services. Operators may agree lower charges, or other port sizes, using TRAI's method. Breaking the rules can cost up to ₹15 lakh per service area for each violation. The old 2012 charges now apply only to E1 ports.

steps.text: Calls and data between two operators pass through ports, and operators pay each other a yearly charge for those ports.
The 2012 rules priced only old E1/TDM ports, so the IP ports networks now use had no framework.
A cap gives every operator a known maximum, which TRAI says brings certainty, transparency and fair competition.
From 1 January 2027 all new interconnections must be IP-based, so IP port prices will matter more over time.

Whether any saving reaches customers is not known.

lesson.big_idea: When your call crosses to another operator's network, it passes through a port. Operators pay each other a yearly fee for each port. A cap sets the most that fee can be.

steps.title: Networks must meet
steps.text: Each operator runs its own network. If you call a friend on a different network, the call must cross into their network at a meeting point called an interconnection.

steps.title: Ports are the doorways
steps.text: At that meeting point, links plug into ports. A port's size is its capacity, measured in Gbps (gigabits per second). A bigger port carries more calls and data at once.

steps.title: Each port carries a yearly fee
steps.text: Operators pay each other a yearly charge for these ports. It is a wholesale cost between companies, not a line on your bill. Port charges were last revised in 2012, for older E1 ports.

steps.title: TRAI sets the ceiling
steps.text: From 1 January 2027, TRAI caps the yearly charge for an IP port at ₹5.6 lakh for 1 Gbps and ₹42.3 lakh for 10 Gbps. Operators may agree lower charges.

steps.title: Spread it over customers
steps.text: An operator's port costs are shared across all its customers. Divide the cost by the number of customers to see the effect per person.

example.setup: Say a small operator needs 10 Gbps of capacity to connect with a rival, and has 10 lakh customers. It can take ten 1 Gbps ports or one 10 Gbps port.

lines.label: Ten small ports
lines.note: Using the 1 Gbps cap.

lines.label: One big port
lines.note: Using the 10 Gbps cap.

lines.label: Saving

lines.label: Per customer

lines.label: Per month
lines.note: A tiny share of a monthly bill.

example.result: Bigger ports cost less per gigabit. Even the full cap, spread across customers, works out to about 35 paise a month. That is why a direct bill change is unlikely.

apply.text: So when TRAI capped IP ports at ₹5.6 lakh and ₹42.3 lakh a year from 1 January 2027, it set the price of the doorways between networks. These are wholesale costs between operators. TRAI says the aim is certainty, transparency and fair competition. No source says tariffs will change.

practice.q: The same operator now needs 20 Gbps. What is the most it pays a year using 10 Gbps ports, and how much does that save over 1 Gbps ports?
practice.answer: Two 10 Gbps ports: 2 × ₹42.3 lakh = ₹84.6 lakh. Twenty 1 Gbps ports: 20 × ₹5.6 lakh = ₹112 lakh. Saving: ₹112 lakh − ₹84.6 lakh = ₹27.4 lakh a year.

sections.title: World
sections.gist: Krakow mourns at least nine dead; Europe joins Ukraine talks; Eisenkot gets Israel's mandate; Trump doubts midterms; COP31 opens.

items.headline: Krakow shooting suspect dies; at least nine dead in two towns
items.text: The 24-year-old man suspected of a shooting in Krakow's Main Square died in hospital on 9 November, Polish police said, DW reports. He was wounded in a shootout with police. Six people were killed in the shooting, and Al Jazeera reports 15 were wounded. Police also found the bodies of three of his family members at their home, the BBC reports. That brings the toll to at least nine people across two towns. The New York Times reports that his motive is still unclear. It is not yet known what investigators will find about why he did it.
items.background: The shooting took place in the Main Square of Krakow, a city in Poland. Police wounded the suspect in an exchange of fire.
items.why: At least nine people died, and with the suspect dead, investigators must explain the motive without questioning him.

items.headline: Europe to join US-led Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi on 10–11 November
items.text: France's foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, said Europeans will be represented at the US-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine. The talks are in Abu Dhabi on 10–11 November, and France will attend. This is a point of dispute. Russia has suggested there would be no place for Europeans at the table. Ukraine's President Zelensky wants European allies involved. The New York Times reports that a ceasefire will not be on the table when the talks resume. Watch whether Russia accepts the Europeans' presence, and what the sides discuss instead of a ceasefire.
items.background: The US is mediating talks between Russia and Ukraine aimed at ending their war. The Abu Dhabi meeting resumes those talks.
items.why: Who sits at the table shapes any deal, and Russia and Ukraine disagree on whether Europe gets a seat.

items.headline: Eisenkot gets first chance to form Israel's next government
items.text: On 8 November Israel's President Herzog formally gave Gadi Eisenkot the first chance to form a government. Eisenkot has 28 days, so until about 6 December, with a possible two-week extension. If he fails, Netanyahu gets a chance. The 27 October election left neither Eisenkot's bloc nor Netanyahu's bloc with a clear majority. So Eisenkot needs partners from outside his bloc. The ultra-Orthodox party UTJ has left the door open to working with him. But UTJ wants draft exemptions kept. These are rules that excuse some people from compulsory military service. Watch whether Eisenkot can win UTJ over without giving way on that demand.
items.background: In Israel, when an election has no clear winner, the president picks one lawmaker to try to build a majority coalition.
items.why: The outcome decides whether Eisenkot or Netanyahu leads Israel's next government.

items.headline: Trump questions midterm results, says deportations may have been too tough
items.text: In remarks reported on 9 November, US President Donald Trump said his deportation policy 'might have been too tough' for voters in the midterm elections, AP reports. NBC News reports that he then cast doubt on the election results, after earlier saying he was 'absolutely willing' to accept them. CNBC reports that he revived a conspiracy theory about voting machines while questioning the results. It is not yet known whether he will take any formal step to challenge a result.
items.background: The US recently held midterm elections, which choose members of Congress halfway through a president's four-year term.
items.why: When a sitting president questions election results, it tests public trust in how US votes are counted.

items.headline: COP31 UN climate summit opens in Antalya, Turkey
items.text: The UN climate summit COP31 opened in Antalya, Turkey, on 9 November. Turkey's Environment Minister Murat Kurum is COP31 President. Australia's Chris Bowen leads the negotiations. UN climate chief Simon Stiell urged countries to deliver the pledges they have already made. The African Group of countries pressed on climate finance, which is money from richer countries to help poorer ones cut emissions and cope with warming. The Globe and Mail says the talks begin against a backdrop of disasters, energy price shocks and rising temperatures. Watch whether countries make new promises, or focus on keeping the ones they already made.
items.background: COP summits are yearly UN meetings where governments negotiate how to slow climate change and who pays for it.
items.why: Deals on climate finance decide how much money richer countries give poorer ones to cope with rising temperatures.

items.headline: Trump says new Iran strikes unlikely, but Gulf attacks go on
items.text: In remarks to CNN reported on 8 November, President Donald Trump said a new US offensive on Iran was 'highly unlikely' to be necessary. He said that depends on Iran signing 'a very strong agreement'. He tied it to talks on Iran's nuclear programme and reopening the Strait of Hormuz. He said US forces were ready, with three aircraft carriers in the region. On 9 November oil fell to a 10-week low. The attacks went on. Reports on 9 November said debris from an intercepted Houthi missile damaged Aramco Tower in Riyadh. Separately, a drone hit a gas storage tank at Iraq's Khor Mor field.
items.background: The US is at war with Iran.
items.why: Mid-2026 reports said India gets about 40% of its oil, half its LNG (liquefied natural gas) and about 90% of its LPG imports through Hormuz.

items.headline: China extends US tariff pause, floats Xi–Trump–Putin meeting
items.text: On 9 November 2026, China announced a two-month extension of its pause on the extra 24% tariff on US goods. The 10% tariff stays in place. The exact end date is not confirmed, but it appears to match the 10 January 2027 date agreed in September. Three days earlier, on 6 November, China confirmed for the first time that talks are under way on a possible Xi–Trump–Putin meeting. Foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said China is in communication with relevant parties. Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said the meeting was being planned for Shenzhen, which hosts the APEC summit in November 2026. Nothing is final, and no agenda is set.
items.background: A tariff is a tax on goods that come in from another country.
items.why: The direct effect on you is small.

sections.title: India
sections.gist: Supreme Court makes suspension automatic after 48 hours' custody; Manipur sends Kuki killings to NIA as court pauses census.

items.headline: Supreme Court: 48 hours in judicial custody means automatic suspension
items.text: The Supreme Court has ruled that a public servant arrested and held in judicial custody for more than 48 hours is "deemed suspended". That means the suspension happens automatically. The department does not need to issue a separate suspension order. Judicial custody means a person is held in jail on a court's orders, not in a police lock-up. LiveLaw reported the ruling on 9 November. The case was Vishwajeet Singh v. State of Bihar, decided by Justices JB Pardiwala and Manmohan. The bench also set aside a Patna High Court order that had cancelled the bail of a Bihar hospital administrator in a bribery case.
items.background: Government employees facing arrest are often suspended from duty. The question was whether a formal order is always required.
items.why: For government employees, more than 48 hours in judicial custody now means automatic suspension, with no separate order.

items.headline: Manipur hands killing of two Kuki youths to the NIA
items.text: On 9 November Manipur Chief Minister Yumnam Khemchand Singh said the killing of two Kuki youths has been handed to the NIA, India's National Investigation Agency. He announced this while meeting their families at Taphou Kuki village in Kangpokpi. Tinginlun Chongloi, 21, and Paoginlal Hangshing, 20, went missing from the village on 28 October. Their bodies were found on 1 November in Senapati district. No arrests have been reported. The group CoTU has suspended its shutdown for seven days. Watch whether the NIA makes arrests before that pause ends.
items.background: Two young Kuki men vanished from a village in Manipur's Kangpokpi area and were later found dead in Senapati district.
items.why: A central agency now leads the case, and a local shutdown is on hold for seven days.

items.headline: Manipur High Court keeps Census 2027 on hold until 30 April 2027
items.text: The Manipur High Court has ordered that Census 2027 in the state stay on hold until 30 April 2027. The order, published on 6 November, cites concerns of displaced residents. Existing census notifications, including the state's 22 March 2026 notification, stay in place and are not withdrawn. The Registrar General, who runs India's census, must decide seven representations, or formal objections, through one "speaking order": a written decision that gives reasons. Anyone may submit a representation by 25 November 2026. After that order, the census stays paused four more weeks so it can be challenged in court. It is not yet known how this affects the national timetable.
items.background: Ethnic violence in Manipur has forced many people from their homes, raising questions about counting them where they now live.
items.why: An accurate count decides funding, welfare and political seats; displaced people risk being missed or wrongly counted.

items.headline: Yogi says 1.27 crore Hindu voters are missing from UP rolls
items.text: UP Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath told a BJP state executive meeting that about 1.27 crore Hindu voters are missing from UP's voter lists. Outlook India reported this on 1 November 2026. He told party workers to work with booth level officers (BLOs) to get these people included. On 6 November Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav asked how the Chief Minister knew this figure. On 9 November The Indian Express reported Yogi saying he has appealed to the EC. No EC response has been reported.
items.background: The Election Commission (EC) has been running SIR, a Special Intensive Revision that re-checks every name on voter lists.
items.why: If you vote in UP, check your name on voters.eci.gov.in.

sections.title: Your money & life
sections.gist: Delhi's air stays near severe after Diwali, the RBI calls the cheque-book rumour fake, and the foreign-asset amnesty closes 31 December.

items.headline: Delhi's air stays near 'severe' after Diwali under Stage III curbs
items.text: Delhi's daily average air quality index (AQI, a 0–500 pollution score) was 376 on Diwali, Sunday 8 November. That was up from 369 on Saturday 7 November. On the morning of Monday 9 November, the city reading was 366 at 6:15 am, but 15 monitoring stations were in the 'severe' range. Stage III of GRAP has applied across Delhi-NCR since 6 November. A CAQM order restricts dust-generating construction and demolition from 5 to 20 November. It also asks offices to cap physical attendance at 50%. Watch whether readings ease or curbs change before 20 November.
items.background: GRAP is Delhi-NCR's stage-by-stage plan against air pollution. Each stage adds curbs as air worsens. CAQM, the air-quality commission, issues the orders.
items.why: Delhi-NCR residents face very poor air, plus limits on construction and office attendance until at least 20 November.

items.headline: RBI: your current cheque books stay valid after 31 December
items.text: A viral social media message claimed banks would issue new CTS cheque books with extra security from 1 January 2027. One version said old cheque leaves would work only for payments up to ₹50,000. Reports on 9 November said the RBI called the message factually incorrect and misleading, and marked the image fake. The RBI said it is not introducing any such measures for CTS cheque books at present. No RBI rule asks you to replace existing CTS cheque books by 31 December 2026. They remain valid. The RBI asks people to rely only on its official communication.
items.background: CTS, the Cheque Truncation System, lets banks clear cheques using scanned images, so the paper cheque does not need to travel.
items.why: You do not need to replace your cheque book. Check any claimed banking rule change against the RBI's own announcements.

items.headline: RBI tightens cyber security rules for payment networks and wallets
items.text: The RBI has issued revised Master Directions on Cyber Resilience and Digital Payment Security Controls, reported on 6 November. They cover non-bank payment operators: NPCI, card networks, payment aggregators, prepaid wallet and card issuers, and white-label ATM operators. The rules replace six earlier circulars. Operators must report cyber incidents to the RBI within six hours. They must audit their systems every year. For critical vendor software, they need access to the source code, or a copy held by a neutral third party (escrow). The 12-hour cooling-off period after you change your registered mobile number or email stays. Large and medium operators must comply immediately; small ones by 1 April 2028.
items.background: NPCI runs UPI. Payment aggregators help shops take online payments. Prepaid issuers run wallets and gift cards. White-label ATMs are run by non-banks.
items.why: These rules govern the firms behind UPI, cards and wallets. The 12-hour cooling-off can slow a fraudster who changes your registered number.

items.headline: Foreign-asset amnesty closes 31 December; taxpayers seek CBDT clarity
items.text: The Economic Times reported on 9 November that taxpayers want the CBDT, India's direct-tax authority, to clarify the disclosure rules in the foreign-asset amnesty scheme. The scheme, FAST-DS 2026, was notified on 14 August and runs until 31 December 2026. It has two routes. Route one covers undisclosed foreign assets up to ₹1 crore: 30% tax plus an equal penalty. So a ₹10 lakh asset would cost ₹3 lakh tax plus ₹3 lakh penalty, or ₹6 lakh. Route two covers assets bought from already-taxed income but left out of return schedules, up to ₹5 crore: a flat ₹1 lakh fee. It is not yet known whether the CBDT will clarify before the deadline.
items.background: An amnesty scheme lets people declare hidden or missed assets on fixed terms within a set window.
items.why: Indian taxpayers with foreign assets missing from their tax returns have until 31 December 2026 to use this window.

sections.title: Markets & money
sections.gist: Oil's biggest weekly fall since 2020 hasn't reached Indian pumps. Foreign funds turn to India as the AI trade wobbles. US inflation data is due 10 November.

items.headline: Brent oil falls nearly 15% in a week; Indian pump prices unchanged
items.text: Brent crude, the global oil price benchmark, fell nearly 15% in the week to 6 November. It settled near $99 a barrel after touching a weekly low of $93.22. Bhaskar English reported on 9 November that this was oil's biggest weekly fall since 2020. Indian pump prices did not move. In Delhi, petrol stayed at ₹102.12 a litre and diesel at ₹95.20. It is not yet known whether fuel retailers will cut prices, or whether the fall in crude will last.
items.background: Indian pump prices include large taxes and are set by fuel retailers, so they do not move day by day with crude.
items.why: Cheaper crude lowers India's oil import bill and could reach petrol and diesel prices if retailers pass it on.

items.headline: Foreign funds move into India as AI share trade falters
items.text: Bloomberg reported on 9 November that foreign funds were piling into India as the 'AI trade' faltered. The AI trade means investors buying shares of companies expected to profit from artificial intelligence. When that bet weakens, some money looks for other markets. The same day, CNBC reported that US stock futures were climbing. Futures are contracts on where an index will go, so they hint at the mood before markets open. CNBC said investors were watching the AI trade and bracing for more economic data and company earnings. Watch those earnings for signs of whether AI bets recover.
items.background: Investors had bet heavily on AI-linked company shares. When such a popular bet weakens, money often moves to other markets.
items.why: Foreign money flowing into Indian shares can lift stock prices and support the rupee.

items.headline: RBI said to question how banks value some bond derivatives
items.text: Bloomberg reported on 9 November that the RBI is said to be querying how banks value some bond derivative trades. A bond derivative is a contract whose value depends on bond prices or interest rates. Banks must record a value for these contracts in their accounts. If a bank sets that value too high, it can look healthier than it really is. It is not yet known which banks or trades are involved. It is also not known whether the RBI will issue new rules.
items.background: The RBI, India's central bank, also supervises banks and checks that their accounts reflect the real risks they carry.
items.why: Correct valuations help ensure banks are not hiding losses that could later hurt their finances.

items.headline: Dollar slips as investors bet on a December Fed hike
items.text: Investing.com reported on 9 November that the US dollar index slipped 0.4% to 101.88. The index measures the dollar against a group of major currencies. The euro rose 0.4% to $1.118. This came after what Investing.com called a 'blowout' US jobs report. Investors are firming up bets that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates in December. The logic: more jobs mean more spending, which can push prices up, so the Fed may raise rates to cool things down. US consumer price data, the main inflation reading, is due on 10 November.
items.background: The Federal Reserve is the US central bank. It raises interest rates to cool prices when the economy runs hot.
items.why: Higher US interest rates can pull investment money out of India and weaken the rupee.

items.headline: Boeing to cut about 5% of its commercial plane workforce
items.text: Boeing said on Monday 9 November that it will cut about 5% of the workforce in its commercial plane business. The cuts will come through layoffs and attrition, which means people who leave are not replaced. Boeing said it is moderating the pace at which it raises jet production. Its executives had already signalled slower plans to raise plane output. The number of people affected was not stated in the reports. It is not yet known how far the production plans will slow.
items.background: Boeing is a major maker of passenger jets and had been working to raise how many planes it builds.
items.why: Slower Boeing production can mean longer waits for new planes for airlines worldwide. No direct effect on India was reported.

sections.title: Tech & AI
sections.gist: Trump and Musk back Nvidia's Huang as the FBI looks at his affair. Apple eyes an agent-like Siri, and the US backlash against data centres grows.

items.headline: Trump and Musk back Nvidia's Jensen Huang after affair admission
items.text: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted, in an email to employees, to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, The Guardian reports. Donald Trump, Elon Musk and prominent finance figures have publicly backed him. AP reported on 9 November that Trump said the FBI is looking at the affair. China rejected the espionage claims. Separately, The New York Times reported that a Commerce Department inquiry into chips was halted after Nvidia intervened. Watch what the FBI does next, and whether questions grow over the halted Commerce inquiry.
items.background: Nvidia makes chips widely used to build AI systems, so its links to China draw close US government attention.
items.why: Questions about Nvidia's CEO and China touch US national security and the rules on selling AI chips.

items.headline: Apple's CEO pushes for bolder AI, possibly an agent-like Siri
items.text: Bloomberg reported on 8 November that Apple's CEO is pressing the company's software chief to pursue a more ambitious AI strategy. Reporter Mark Gurman said Apple could make Siri more like an agent as early as 2027. An AI agent does not just answer questions. It carries out multi-step tasks for you across apps. These are media reports, not an Apple announcement. What an agent-like Siri would do, and when it would arrive, is not yet known.
items.background: Siri is the voice assistant built into iPhones and other Apple devices.
items.why: Apple's AI choices decide what iPhone users, including in India, can hand off to their phones.

items.headline: Local fights over AI data centres feed a wider US backlash
items.text: Politico reported on 8 November that local fights over data centres are fuelling a wider backlash in the US. Data centres are large buildings full of computers that run AI tools and online services. Mashable reported the same day on Harwood, North Dakota. It described Harwood as possibly the only US town to vote yes on data centres in this wave of local fights. Watch whether more towns vote on data centres, and which way they go.
items.background: AI companies need more and more data centres, and some residents oppose having them built nearby.
items.why: Where data centres can be built affects how fast AI services can grow.

sections.title: Science, health & climate
sections.gist: NASA brings a crewed Moon landing forward to 2028, Lilly's obesity pill eases sleep apnea, and a Hyderabad startup bets on cancer vaccines.

items.headline: NASA plans a crewed Moon landing in 2028, with a 2027 rehearsal
items.text: NASA has set out a faster plan to land astronauts on the Moon in 2028. That landing is Artemis IV, which uses the SLS rocket and the Orion spacecraft. First comes Artemis III in 2027. Four astronauts will spend 14 days in Earth orbit, not at the Moon. They will practise meeting and docking with test versions of two competing Moon landers, one from SpaceX and one from Blue Origin. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said the campaign must move with urgency, because strategic competitors are pursuing a permanent presence beyond Earth. Next to watch: whether both landers are ready for the 2027 orbital test.
items.background: Artemis is NASA's programme to return people to the Moon. SLS is its large rocket, and Orion is the capsule that carries the crew.
items.why: Practising docking in Earth orbit first lowers risk before astronauts attempt the far harder trip to the lunar surface.

items.headline: Lilly's obesity pill Foundayo eased sleep apnea in two large trials
items.text: On 9 November Eli Lilly said its pill Foundayo (orforglipron) significantly reduced the severity of obstructive sleep apnea. The results come from Phase 3 trials, the final large stage of testing before approval. The trials, called ATTAIN-OSA, enrolled adults with obesity or overweight. STAT reported that the pill helped in two late-stage studies. Foundayo is a GLP-1 pill, from the same drug family as popular weight-loss injections, but taken by mouth. CNBC reported the results pave the way for approval for sleep apnea. Next: Lilly plans to file with the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) by the end of 2026.
items.background: In obstructive sleep apnea, the airway repeatedly blocks during sleep, so breathing stops and starts. Extra body weight makes it more likely.
items.why: Nothing changes in India yet. Lilly is first seeking approval from the FDA, the US drug regulator.

items.headline: Hyderabad startup PopVax bets on custom-made cancer mRNA vaccines
items.text: On 9 November ThePrint reported that Hyderabad-based PopVax is betting on personalised cancer mRNA vaccines priced at ₹2.7 crore per patient. PopVax opened its RNA Foundry in Hyderabad on 31 October 2026. It aims to make more than 100 personalised cancer vaccine candidates over the next 12 months. The company estimates most projects take about 8–10 weeks and cost around USD 300,000 each. That is roughly two months of work to design and make one vaccine for one patient. Still unknown: how well these candidates will work, and who will be able to pay for them.
items.background: An mRNA vaccine gives cells instructions to make a protein. A personalised cancer vaccine targets proteins found only in one patient's tumour.
items.why: An Indian company is building this technology at home, but at ₹2.7 crore per patient, cost is the big question.

sections.title: Formula 1
sections.gist: A post-race penalty drops Leclerc to eighth in Brazil, Verstappen climbs from 21st to second, and Piastri parts ways with manager Webber.

items.headline: Brazil penalty drops Leclerc to eighth; Verstappen goes 21st to second
items.text: After the Brazilian Grand Prix, the stewards (the race officials) gave Ferrari's Charles Leclerc a five-second penalty. It was for his clash with Liam Lawson on lap 69. The penalty dropped Leclerc to eighth, and Lawson moved up to seventh. Kimi Antonelli and Oliver Bearman were also punished for unsafe releases from the pit lane. Neither penalty changed their places: Antonelli stayed fifth and Bearman 17th. The bigger story was Max Verstappen. He started 21st and finished second. Motorsport.com said it was his third impressive comeback drive in Brazil in three years.
items.background: A time penalty is added to a driver's race time, so a driver who finishes close to rivals can lose places.
items.why: Penalties decided after the race can still change the final order and the points each team takes home.

items.headline: Oscar Piastri and Mark Webber end their management partnership
items.text: On 9 November McLaren driver Oscar Piastri and former F1 driver Mark Webber said they had mutually agreed to end their management deal. Webber and his wife Ann had managed Piastri since 2019. That is about seven years, covering his rise into Formula 1. Webber said the reason was his reduced trackside involvement this season. Piastri will move to a new management structure. Who will run it has not been named. Next to watch: who takes over his contract talks and business deals.
items.background: A driver's manager negotiates contracts and sponsorships and often guides career choices, such as which team to join.
items.why: Piastri's next manager will shape his future contract talks, a key factor for any top driver.

sections.title: Cricket — the masala
sections.gist: India can seal the New Zealand ODI series at Hamilton, Rodrigues returns for South Africa, and Scotland limits matches against Afghanistan.

items.headline: India can seal the New Zealand ODI series at Hamilton
items.text: India lead New Zealand 2-0 in the five-match ODI series. A win in the third ODI at Hamilton would seal it, with two games to spare. The Hindu says the batting is less settled than the scoreline. Apart from Virat Kohli's knock at Eden Park, no Indian batter has looked comfortable. That includes captain Shubman Gill and Rohit Sharma, who is in focus. After this match, the coaching staff splits. Head coach Gautam Gambhir stays with the ODI squad. Kotak and Morkel join the Test team in Wellington. A Test preparation camp begins on 11 November, and pacers Arshdeep Singh, Gurnoor Brar and Auqib Nabi stay back for it.
items.background: India are touring New Zealand for five one-day internationals (ODIs), with Test matches also on the trip.
items.why: Splitting coaches and players shows India running ODI and Test preparation side by side on one tour.

items.headline: Jemimah Rodrigues and Amanjot Kaur return for India's South Africa tour
items.text: India's women's squads for South Africa were reported on 9 November. Jemimah Rodrigues and Amanjot Kaur return after injuries. Rodrigues is in both squads: the ODIs, which are 50-over matches, and the T20Is, which are 20-over matches. She recently came back in domestic T20 cricket and scored a century for Mumbai. Renuka Singh Thakur is picked only for the T20Is, not the ODIs. The reports do not say why.
items.background: Selectors pick separate squads for ODIs and T20Is, so a player can be chosen for one format but not the other.
items.why: Two players back from injury give India's selectors more choices for the South Africa series.

items.headline: Scotland will play Afghanistan only at ICC events
items.text: On 9 November Cricket Scotland announced it is reducing its cricket relations with Afghanistan. The decision followed a review by its board of how the two countries engage. From now on, Scotland will only play Afghanistan at ICC events. Those are tournaments run by the International Cricket Council, the sport's world governing body. This means no separate series between the two teams outside those events. The report did not give the board's detailed reasons. It is not yet known whether other boards will take similar steps.
items.background: Teams play each other in two ways: in their own arranged series, and in tournaments run by the ICC.
items.why: It shows how a board can cut regular contact with a team while still facing it at world events.

quiz.q: China's factory input costs rose 7.9% but factory selling prices rose 5.7%. What does this tell you?
options: Factories are absorbing part of the cost rise, so their margins are squeezed
Chinese shoppers are now paying 7.9% more for goods
Chinese factories are earning record profits
quiz.why: Costs rose faster than selling prices, so the gap per unit shrank. Shoppers saw only a 0.7% rise.

quiz.q: Which change would most likely have protected a store's fridges in this attack?

Buying newer, larger freezers for the store
Locking the store's doors at night
quiz.why: The attack worked because the panels could be reached online and ran outdated firmware. Fixing either problem closes the way in.
